headline: US Navy uses Xbox-style controllers to fire anti-drone lasers on warships
summary: The familiar controllers offer targeting precision and rapid input, making them ideal for operating advanced weapon platforms now deployed on warships and used in active conflict zones.
details: The U.S. Navy has adopted Xbox-style controllers to operate anti-drone laser systems on its warships. This choice leverages the controllers' ergonomic design for targeting precision and rapid user inputs, alongside sailors' existing familiarity with the layout.

These aren't experimental systems; they are deployed on warships and have reportedly been used against drones in the Strait of Hormuz. Lasers offer a highly cost-effective solution, with an estimated $13 per engagement compared to thousands for traditional missiles.

Unlike conventional ammunition, laser weapons only require electrical power, allowing for sustained defense against threats as long as the vessel has sufficient power. This capability extends a ship's defensive capacity long after it might run out of missiles or ammo.

While specific details like wired/wireless connection or custom vs. off-the-shelf controllers remain undisclosed, this isn't the first instance of gaming controllers in critical systems. The ill-fated Titan submersible famously used a Logitech F710 controller.

headline_marked: [[TypeSafe AI's Jev sparks two-week clone war]] with non-generative AI
headline: TypeSafe AI's Jev sparks two-week clone war with non-generative AI
summary: Jev, a discriminative AI model from TypeSafe AI, offers fast, probability-based verdicts without generating text. Its unique approach led to clones from OpenAI and AWS within two weeks.
details: TypeSafe AI launched Jev on September 15, 2026, founded by Diogo Almeida, who previously worked on ChatGPT's instruction-following at OpenAI. Jev is not a generative model but a discriminative one, designed to classify and score.

Users send program state and typed questions to Jev, receiving probabilities back in 70 to 500 milliseconds. Crucially, Jev never writes text and output tokens cost nothing, making it distinct from traditional generative AI.

The release quickly led to a "clone war"; within two weeks, OpenAI shipped a Decisions API built on its Luna model, and AWS released a local model called Strands Decider 2B. TechCrunch reported on Amazon's "Jev clone" as decision models flooded the web.

This shift matters because if the next phase of AI involves models that stop generating text, the way AI agents are built will fundamentally change. Jev's approach challenges the common perception of AI as solely text generators.

Jev is a discriminative model that classifies and scores inputs, answering multiple questions in parallel in a single call. Its vocabulary is limited to three primitives, focusing on verdicts rather than open-ended generation.
The speed comes from Jev skipping token generation; unlike normal models that emit one token at a time, Jev samples every answer at once, in parallel, leveraging hardware awareness for efficiency.

Its training uses Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD), which optimizes for honest probabilities. This means high confidence directly correlates with high accuracy, making the model's numerical outputs highly trustworthy for integration into systems.

Despite its innovations, Jev has faced criticism, with some on r/LocalLLaMA calling it "old tech" and a classifier with calibrated probabilities a "solved problem." TypeSafe AI has also not published enough architecture detail to verify all its claims.

Input tokens cost $0.042 per million, with output tokens being free, a pricing model TypeSafe admits might be subsidized. Jev also has a documented gap: it lacks deep knowledge of niche domains, requiring users to supply context.

Beyond big tech, Jev found strange adoption in roleplay communities like r/SillyTavernAI, where it scores chat replies for character consistency at low cost. Builders also integrated it into Claude Code memory tooling and Cloudflare Workers.

Jev is named after Daniel Kahneman's System 1, representing fast, intuitive thinking. This marks a pendulum swing in AI product naming, moving from "System 2 reasoning" marketing to models focused on rapid, decisive verdicts.
